claim: Adult neurogenesis provides the dentate gyrus with a heterogeneous population of granule cells (GCs) that were born and developed their properties at different times.
source: Adult neurogenesis provides the dentate gyrus with a heterogeneous population of granule cells (GCs) that were born and developed their properties at different times.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological process of adult neurogenesis and its effect on the dentate gyrus population, drawing from established scientific knowledge about neurogenesis.

claim: Immature GCs have distinct intrinsic and synaptic properties than mature GCs.
source: Immature GCs have distinct intrinsic and synaptic properties than mature GCs and are needed for correct encoding and discrimination in spatial tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing these differences.

claim: Immature GCs are needed for correct encoding and discrimination in spatial tasks.
source: Immature GCs have distinct intrinsic and synaptic properties than mature GCs and are needed for correct encoding and discrimination in spatial tasks.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Immature GCs produce unreliable responses compared to mature GCs, exhibiting imprecise spike timings across repeated stimulation.
source: Immature GCs produce unreliable responses compared to mature GCs, exhibiting imprecise spike timings across repeated stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing reliability measurements across different GC ages.

claim: Immature GCs perform a differential encoding of stimuli.
source: Parameter values from this fit reflect the maturational differences of the population and indicate that immature GCs perform a differential encoding of stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical model parameters obtained from fitting the spike response model to experimental data.

claim: Despite their individual unreliability, immature GCs enhance the fidelity of the signal encoded by the population.
source: We find that, despite their individual unreliability, immature GCs enhance the fidelity of the signal encoded by the population and improve the discrimination of similar time-dependent stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis using populations of simulated granule cells.

claim: Immature GCs improve the discrimination of similar time-dependent stimuli.
source: We find that, despite their individual unreliability, immature GCs enhance the fidelity of the signal encoded by the population and improve the discrimination of similar time-dependent stimuli.
evidence: This is demonstrated through pattern separation tasks performed with simulated populations.

claim: New neurons termed granule cells (GCs) are born beyond development in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
source: In the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus, cell diversity is enhanced and structured by adult neurogenesis, a mechanism by which new neurons termed granule cells (GCs) are born beyond development (van Praag et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Praag et al., 2002.

claim: Adult-born GCs mature in a stereotyped way, making a distinctive contribution to hippocampal function during maturation.
source: These adult-born GCs mature in a stereotyped way, making a distinctive contribution to hippocampal function during maturation (Danielson et al., 2016; Clelland et al., 2009; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: After about 8 weeks, adult-born GCs become electrophysiologically indistinguishable from other mature neurons.
source: After about 8 weeks, they become electrophysiologically indistinguishable from other mature neurons (Laplagne et al., 2006; Mongiat et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laplagne et al., 2006 and Mongiat et al., 2009.

claim: About 4 weeks after cell birth, immature GCs establish functional synapses that can activate postsynaptic targets in CA3.
source: About 4 weeks after cell birth, immature GCs establish functional synapses that can activate postsynaptic targets in CA3 (Toni et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2012; Temprana et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: At 4 weeks of age, immature GCs receive presynaptic inputs from within the hippocampus.
source: At this age, they also receive presynaptic inputs from within the hippocampus (Vivar et al., 2012), the septum (Vivar et al., 2012; Ogando et al., 2021), and the entorhinal cortex (van Praag et al., 2002; Mongiat et al., 2009; Toni et al., 2007; Vivar et al., 2012; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vivar et al., 2012.

claim: At 4 weeks of age, immature GCs receive presynaptic inputs from the septum.
source: At this age, they also receive presynaptic inputs from within the hippocampus (Vivar et al., 2012), the septum (Vivar et al., 2012; Ogando et al., 2021), and the entorhinal cortex (van Praag et al., 2002; Mongiat et al., 2009; Toni et al., 2007; Vivar et al., 2012; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vivar et al., 2012 and Ogando et al., 2021.

claim: At 4 weeks of age, immature GCs receive presynaptic inputs from the entorhinal cortex.
source: At this age, they also receive presynaptic inputs from within the hippocampus (Vivar et al., 2012), the septum (Vivar et al., 2012; Ogando et al., 2021), and the entorhinal cortex (van Praag et al., 2002; Mongiat et al., 2009; Toni et al., 2007; Vivar et al., 2012; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: 4-week-old GCs exhibit different electrophysiological properties from those of mature GCs, such as an increased excitation/inhibition balance.
source: Experiments in hippocampal slices have shown that 4-week-old GCs (4wGCs) exhibit different electrophysiological properties from those of mature GCs (mGCs), such as an increased excitation/inhibition balance, a higher membrane excitability, a slower membrane time constant, and lower action potential threshold (Mongiat et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a; Temprana et al., 2015; Pardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: 4-week-old GCs exhibit a higher membrane excitability than mature GCs.
source: Experiments in hippocampal slices have shown that 4-week-old GCs (4wGCs) exhibit different electrophysiological properties from those of mature GCs (mGCs), such as an increased excitation/inhibition balance, a higher membrane excitability, a slower membrane time constant, and lower action potential threshold (Mongiat et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a; Temprana et al., 2015; Pardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: 4-week-old GCs exhibit a slower membrane time constant than mature GCs.
source: Experiments in hippocampal slices have shown that 4-week-old GCs (4wGCs) exhibit different electrophysiological properties from those of mature GCs (mGCs), such as an increased excitation/inhibition balance, a higher membrane excitability, a slower membrane time constant, and lower action potential threshold (Mongiat et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a; Temprana et al., 2015; Pardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: 4-week-old GCs exhibit a lower action potential threshold than mature GCs.
source: Experiments in hippocampal slices have shown that 4-week-old GCs (4wGCs) exhibit different electrophysiological properties from those of mature GCs (mGCs), such as an increased excitation/inhibition balance, a higher membrane excitability, a slower membrane time constant, and lower action potential threshold (Mongiat et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a; Temprana et al., 2015; Pardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: Around 4 weeks after cell birth, immature GCs become integrated into the hippocampal circuitry and could play a distinctive role in the encoding and transmission of information.
source: Therefore, around 4 weeks after cell birth, immature GCs become integrated into the hippocampal circuitry and could play a distinctive role in the encoding and transmission of information.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about connectivity and electrophysiological properties.

claim: In vivo, immature GCs fire at higher rates than mature GCs.
source: In vivo, immature GCs exhibit distinctive patterns of activity: they fire at higher rates, they are less spatially tuned, and are preferentially activated during spatial memory tasks (Danielson et al., 2016; Kee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: In vivo, immature GCs are less spatially tuned than mature GCs.
source: In vivo, immature GCs exhibit distinctive patterns of activity: they fire at higher rates, they are less spatially tuned, and are preferentially activated during spatial memory tasks (Danielson et al., 2016; Kee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: Immature GCs are preferentially activated during spatial memory tasks.
source: In vivo, immature GCs exhibit distinctive patterns of activity: they fire at higher rates, they are less spatially tuned, and are preferentially activated during spatial memory tasks (Danielson et al., 2016; Kee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: Immature GCs promote pattern separation.
source: Immature GCs also promote pattern separation, a computation usually associated with the dentate gyrus which presumably involves augmenting the differences between similar incoming activity before relaying it (Leutgeb et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leutgeb et al., 2007.

claim: Pattern separation involves augmenting the differences between similar incoming activity before relaying it.
source: Immature GCs also promote pattern separation, a computation usually associated with the dentate gyrus which presumably involves augmenting the differences between similar incoming activity before relaying it (Leutgeb et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Leutgeb et al., 2007.

claim: Ablating or inhibiting immature GCs impairs pattern separation.
source: Behavioral experiments have shown that ablating or inhibiting immature GCs impairs pattern separation (Danielson et al., 2016; Clelland et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin and Schinder, 2012b), while enhancing neurogenesis or inhibiting mGCs' outputs improves it (Nakashiba et al., 2012; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral experiments.

claim: Enhancing neurogenesis improves pattern separation.
source: Behavioral experiments have shown that ablating or inhibiting immature GCs impairs pattern separation (Danielson et al., 2016; Clelland et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin and Schinder, 2012b), while enhancing neurogenesis or inhibiting mGCs' outputs improves it (Nakashiba et al., 2012; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral experiments.

claim: Inhibiting mature GCs' outputs improves pattern separation.
source: Behavioral experiments have shown that ablating or inhibiting immature GCs impairs pattern separation (Danielson et al., 2016; Clelland et al., 2009; Marín-Burgin and Schinder, 2012b), while enhancing neurogenesis or inhibiting mGCs' outputs improves it (Nakashiba et al., 2012; Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral experiments.

claim: The input resistance of GCs decreased with age.
source: Both the input resistance and the time constant measured in this way decreased with age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports (Mongiat et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous reports.

claim: The time constant of GCs decreased with age.
source: Both the input resistance and the time constant measured in this way decreased with age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous reports (Mongiat et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous reports.

claim: When injected with depolarizing current steps, immature GCs fired at higher frequencies than mature ones for the same step amplitude.
source: Additionally, when injected with depolarizing current steps, immature GCs fired at higher frequencies than mature ones for the same step amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lag of the cross-correlation peak between stimulus and response was negatively correlated with age.
source: The lag and the value at the peak of the cross-correlation were negatively and positively correlated with age respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The value at the peak of the cross-correlation between stimulus and response was positively correlated with age.
source: The lag and the value at the peak of the cross-correlation were negatively and positively correlated with age respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GCs' responses become faster with maturation.
source: These results indicate that GCs' responses become faster with maturation and exhibit stronger alignment with the stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-correlation analysis showing decreased lag with age.

claim: GCs' responses exhibit stronger alignment with the stimulus with maturation.
source: These results indicate that GCs' responses become faster with maturation and exhibit stronger alignment with the stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-correlation analysis showing increased peak value with age.

claim: Older pairs of GCs exhibited larger coincidence ratios, indicating their responses were more similar to each other.
source: Older pairs of GCs exhibited larger coincidence ratios, indicating their responses were more similar to each other.
evidence: This is supported by the coincidence ratio analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Immature GCs are less aligned with the stimulus and produce less reliable responses than mature ones.
source: Thus, our data indicates that immature GCs are less aligned with the stimulus and produce less reliable responses than mature ones.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data on cross-correlation and reliability.

claim: Neurons with longer time constants tend to be less reliable.
source: Slower membranes could partly explain the observed unreliability of immature GCs, as neurons with longer time constants tend to be less reliable (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: While mGCs' membranes tended to hyperpolarize after a spike, this effect was generally smaller for immature GCs.
source: While mGCs' membranes tended to hyperpolarize after a spike, this effect was generally smaller for immature GCs (Figure 2D, K).
evidence: This is supported by data from the SRM fitting shown in Figure 2D and K.

claim: The hyperpolarization after a spike in mGCs could be attributed to spike-triggered potassium currents, which have been reported to be smaller in immature GCs.
source: This hyperpolarization could be attributed to spike-triggered potassium currents, which have been reported to be smaller in immature GCs (Mongiat et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to previous studies.

claim: SRM parameters could be used to classify mGCs and 4wGCs with cross-validated accuracies of 0.72 and 0.75, respectively.
source: SRM parameters could be used to classify mGCs and 4wGCs with cross-validated accuracies of 0.72 and 0.75, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by linear discriminant analysis performed on the SRM parameters.

claim: The classification accuracy of 5wGCs was 0.47, with a fraction of 0.41 5wGCs being classified as 4wGCs.
source: The other 0.28 and 0.25 fractions were classified as 5wGCs indicating that 4wGCs and mGCs were very well discriminated by the LDA. Being maturationally in between, the classification accuracy of 5wGCs was 0.47, with a fraction of 0.41 5wGCs being classified as 4wGCs.
evidence: This is supported by linear discriminant analysis performed on the SRM parameters.

claim: 5wGCs were closer in parameter space to 4wGCs than to mGCs.
source: This suggests that 5wGCs were closer in parameter space to 4wGCs than to mGCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the LDA classification results.

claim: mGCs have a smaller input resistance than immature GCs.
source: We observed that mGCs have a smaller input resistance, a faster membrane, and experience stronger postspike refractory effects.
evidence: This is a summary of the SRM fitting results.

claim: mGCs have a faster membrane than immature GCs.
source: We observed that mGCs have a smaller input resistance, a faster membrane, and experience stronger postspike refractory effects.
evidence: This is a summary of the SRM fitting results.

claim: mGCs experience stronger postspike refractory effects than immature GCs.
source: We observed that mGCs have a smaller input resistance, a faster membrane, and experience stronger postspike refractory effects.
evidence: This is a summary of the SRM fitting results.

claim: The minimum uncertainty about the stimulus before a spike was reduced more in mGCs.
source: Averaging over spikes and GCs, we found that the minimum uncertainty about the stimulus before a spike was reduced more in mGCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Immature SGCs benefit more from using multiple trials for decoding as a consequence of their noisier responses.
source: Immature SGCs benefit more from using multiple trials for decoding as a consequence of their noisier responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of decoding with multiple trials.

claim: Immature GCs produce less precise reconstructions and convey less information about the stimulus.
source: Our results indicate that immature GCs produce less precise reconstructions and convey less information about the stimulus, suggesting that they produce generally worse stimuli representations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the decoding analyses.

claim: mGCs mostly increase decoding performance when paired with other mGCs rather than with immature ones.
source: Moreover, mGCs mostly increase decoding performance when paired with other mGCs rather than with immature ones.
evidence: This is supported by the pair decoding analysis.

claim: From the third step onward in the greedy procedure, immature SGCs were chosen with increasing preference.
source: Unexpectedly, from the third step onward, immature SGCs were chosen by the greedy procedure with increasing preference (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the greedy population construction analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For populations of 12 SGCs, approximately 43% were mSGCs, 32% were 5wSGCs, and 25% were 4wSGCs.
source: For populations of 12 SGCs, approximately 43% were mSGCs, 32% were 5wSGCs, and 25% were 4wSGCs.
evidence: This is supported by the greedy population construction analysis.

claim: 51% of all the SGCs were never chosen in any population by the greedy algorithm.
source: We found that 51% of all the SGCs were never chosen in any population by the greedy algorithm, 34.5% of the SGCs were selected between 1 and 10 times, and 14.5% were selected over 10 times (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the greedy selection shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Decoding performance is a result of a non-trivial synergy between the GCs composing a population.
source: These observations indicate that decoding performance is a result of a non-trivial synergy between the GCs composing a population, and optimal performance is not achieved by taking the best individual GCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that highly selected SGCs did not always perform well individually.

claim: Optimal performance is not achieved by taking the best individual GCs.
source: These observations indicate that decoding performance is a result of a non-trivial synergy between the GCs composing a population, and optimal performance is not achieved by taking the best individual GCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the greedy population construction results.

claim: Mixed-age populations resulted in a steady average decrease in the relative reconstruction error, reaching a final relative improvement of 3%.
source: This resulted in a steady average decrease in the relative reconstruction error, reaching a final relative improvement of 3% (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The populations of mSGCs achieved larger information values than the mixed-age ones.
source: However, the populations of mSGCs achieved larger information values than the mixed-age ones (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In the presence of theta rhythms, stimulus decoding was also improved by the presence of immature SGCs.
source: In the presence of theta rhythms, stimulus decoding was also improved by the presence of immature SGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis with theta-modulated stimuli shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: While single mGCs perform better than immature ones, mixed-age populations improve stimulus reconstruction.
source: Thus, while single mGCs perform better than immature ones, mixed-age populations improve stimulus reconstruction, suggesting that the diversity contributed by immature GCs could be beneficial for transmitting distinct properties of stimuli with rich temporal structure.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the population decoding analyses.

claim: The diversity contributed by immature GCs could be beneficial for transmitting distinct properties of stimuli with rich temporal structure.
source: Thus, while single mGCs perform better than immature ones, mixed-age populations improve stimulus reconstruction, suggesting that the diversity contributed by immature GCs could be beneficial for transmitting distinct properties of stimuli with rich temporal structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the population decoding results.

claim: Ablating neurogenesis affects fine spatial discrimination when the separation between patterns is small, but not when it is large.
source: Ablating neurogenesis affects fine spatial discrimination, that is when the separation between patterns is small, but not when it is large (Clelland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clelland et al., 2009.

claim: For high separation the two stimuli are easily discriminated with almost 100% accuracy both by the mixed-age and mature-only populations.
source: For high separation the two stimuli are easily discriminated with almost 100% accuracy both by the mixed-age and mature-only populations.
evidence: This is supported by the pattern discrimination analysis.

claim: For medium degree of separation the mixed-age populations outperformed the mature-only at the discrimination task.
source: However, for medium degree of separation the mixed-age populations outperformed the mature-only at the discrimination task, suggesting that age heterogeneity in the dentate gyrus could also be leveraged to separate time-varying stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the pattern discrimination analysis.

claim: Age heterogeneity in the dentate gyrus could be leveraged to separate time-varying stimuli.
source: However, for medium degree of separation the mixed-age populations outperformed the mature-only at the discrimination task, suggesting that age heterogeneity in the dentate gyrus could also be leveraged to separate time-varying stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern discrimination results.

claim: Adding noise is detrimental to discrimination performance for the populations.
source: For a fixed degree of separation between the pairs of stimuli, adding noise is detrimental to discrimination performance for the populations (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the noise corruption analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The mixed-age populations consistently outperform the mature-only for moderate amounts of noise.
source: Notably, the mixed-age populations consistently outperform the mature-only for moderate amounts of noise.
evidence: This is supported by the noise corruption analysis.

claim: Immature GCs in the dentate gyrus introduce a degree of heterogeneity at the population level that can be leveraged to reconstruct an incoming stimulus better and discriminate it from others.
source: In summary, our results suggest that immature GCs in the dentate gyrus introduce a degree of heterogeneity at the population level that can be leveraged to reconstruct an incoming stimulus better and, at the same time, discriminate it from others.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the population decoding and discrimination analyses.

claim: Neurogenesis contributes a substantial number of GCs to the dentate gyrus.
source: Neurogenesis contributes a substantial number of GCs to the dentate gyrus (Imayoshi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imayoshi et al., 2008.

claim: Recording from immature GCs in vivo is challenging.
source: However, experimental studies that address questions related to coding are scarce for immature GCs, partly because recording from immature GCs in vivo is challenging.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges in the field.

claim: Immature GCs integrate stimuli over longer time scales than mature GCs.
source: We find that immature GCs integrate stimuli over longer time scales and exhibit weaker refractory effects.
evidence: This is supported by the SRM fitting results.

claim: Immature GCs exhibit weaker refractory effects than mature GCs.
source: We find that immature GCs integrate stimuli over longer time scales and exhibit weaker refractory effects.
evidence: This is supported by the SRM fitting results.

claim: SRM parameters can be used to discriminate GCs' ages.
source: We show that these parameters can be used to discriminate GCs' ages.
evidence: This is supported by the linear discriminant analysis.

claim: Stimulus reconstruction and information improve with maturation when decoding stimuli from the responses of single SGCs.
source: Decoding stimuli from the responses of single SGCs, we find that stimulus reconstruction and information improve with maturation.
evidence: This is supported by the single-cell decoding analysis.

claim: Despite the worse individual performance of immature SGCs, they aid decoding in a simulated population.
source: Unexpectedly, despite the worse individual performance of immature SGCs, we find that they aid decoding in a simulated population.
evidence: This is supported by the population decoding analysis.

claim: Immature SGCs enhance discrimination of highly correlated stimuli.
source: Finally, we use these populations in a pattern separation task to probe the contribution of immature GCs to the discrimination of time-varying stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the pattern discrimination analysis.

claim: Immature GCs' responses are less controlled by inhibitory circuits than mGCs, spiking in response to weaker stimuli and with more variable timing.
source: Immature GCs' responses are less controlled by inhibitory circuits than mGCs, spiking in response to weaker stimuli and with more variable timing (Marín-Burgin et al., 2012a; Pardi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At 4 weeks immature GCs are contacting their postsynaptic targets, but the connections are still maturing so there may still be differences in the strength of the synapses.
source: In addition, although at 4 weeks immature GCs are contacting their postsynaptic targets, the connections are still maturing so there may still be differences in the strength of the synapses (Toni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Toni et al., 2008.

claim: The differences in reliability observed in hippocampal slices could be further increased by the network in vivo.
source: Thus, the differences in reliability that we report here could be further increased by the network.
evidence: This is speculation based on the in vitro findings and knowledge of network effects.

claim: Immature GCs low reliability can be partly attributed to their longer time scales of stimulus integration.
source: We find that immature GCs low reliability can be partly attributed to their longer time scales of stimulus integration.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between time constant and reliability.

claim: Reliable neurons generally achieve better decoding performance.
source: By decoding stimuli with single SGCs and populations, we find that reliable neurons generally achieve better decoding performance and that optimal populations combine diversity with homogeneity, using neurons with different properties while often including the same neuron multiple times.
evidence: This is supported by the decoding analysis.

claim: Optimal populations combine diversity with homogeneity, using neurons with different properties while often including the same neuron multiple times.
source: By decoding stimuli with single SGCs and populations, we find that reliable neurons generally achieve better decoding performance and that optimal populations combine diversity with homogeneity, using neurons with different properties while often including the same neuron multiple times.
evidence: This is supported by the greedy population construction analysis.

claim: In the hippocampus, the postsynaptic area is constantly receiving new synapses from 4-week-old immature cells.
source: In the hippocampus, the postsynaptic area is constantly receiving new synapses from 4-week-old immature cells.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of neurogenesis and synapse formation.

claim: New connections from immature cells may continuously reshape input processing in the postsynaptic area.
source: These new connections may continuously reshape input processing in the area.
evidence: This is speculation based on the continuous addition of new synapses.

claim: Immature GCs are less spatially tuned but actively participate in context encoding and discrimination.
source: Correspondingly, a previous study involving spatial exploration has shown that immature GCs are less spatially tuned but actively participate in context encoding and discrimination (Danielson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Danielson et al., 2016.

claim: Immature GCs fire at higher rates in vivo.
source: Additionally, they reported that immature GCs fire at higher rates in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A higher firing rate would further improve the decoding performance of immature GCs and increase their importance in population coding.
source: In this study, we equalize the firing rates of different neurons, yet a higher firing rate would further improve the decoding performance of immature GCs and increase their importance in population coding.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between firing rate and decoding performance.

claim: Mixed-age populations are able to discriminate between highly correlated stimuli better than exclusively mature populations, even in the presence of uncorrelated noise in the population.
source: Despite immature GCs' variable responses, we find that mixed-age populations are able to discriminate between highly correlated stimuli better than exclusively mature populations, even in the presence of uncorrelated noise in the population.
evidence: This is supported by the pattern discrimination analysis with noise.

claim: The noisier output of immature GCs could help disrupt established memories, consistent with the hypothesis that neurogenesis induces forgetting of existing memories, facilitating the formation of new conflicting ones.
source: The noisier output of immature GCs that we observe could also help disrupt established memories, consistent with the hypothesis that neurogenesis induces forgetting of existing memories, facilitating the formation of new conflicting ones (Epp et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed noisier output and citation to Epp et al., 2016.

claim: Computational studies propose that neurogenesis could prevent interference between new and old memories and aid their discrimination.
source: Using networks that continually incorporate new GCs to encode novel information, these studies propose that neurogenesis could prevent interference between new and old memories and aiding their discrimination.
evidence: This is a summary of computational modeling studies.

claim: Many immature GCs that were highly selected in the populations did not perform well individually in decoding the stimulus.
source: We explored the properties of selected individual GCs and found that many immature GCs that were highly selected in the populations did not perform well individually in decoding the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of individual GC performance.

claim: It is possible that immature GCs' code aspects of the stimulus that are not represented in mature cells.
source: It is possible that immature GCs' code aspects of the stimulus that are not represented in mature cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the population effects.

claim: Immature neurons may modulate mGCs' activity improving stimulus reconstruction, for example by recruiting inhibitory circuits.
source: In addition to individually contributing to decoding, immature neurons may modulate mGCs' activity improving stimulus reconstruction, for example by recruiting inhibitory circuits (Temprana et al., 2015; Anacker and Hen, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to studies on circuit interactions.

claim: The intrinsic diversity of immature GCs contribute to the dentate gyrus could be, by itself, beneficial for stimulus representation and discrimination.
source: Particularly, our study indicates that the intrinsic diversity of immature GCs contribute to the dentate gyrus could be, by itself, beneficial for stimulus representation and discrimination.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.
